before.name: Question 1
before.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+4y=7.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.

Consider the first-order linear ODE dydx+4y=7. We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form
 
u(x)e−3x
u(x)e4x
u(x)e7x
u(x)e−7x
u(x)e−4x
.

Solving for u, we have u(x)=
 
74e4x
73e3x
74e−4x
7e4x
14e4x
.

Therefore, the particular solution is yp(x)=
 
7e−4x
74
74e4x
14
−74
.
Submit

decision.explanation: The homogeneous solution is Ce^{-4x}, so VOP sets y_p=u(x)e^{-4x}. Substitution gives u'(x)e^{-4x}=7, hence u'=7e^{4x} and we may choose u=(7/4)e^{4x}. Therefore y_p=7/4, which satisfies y_p'+4y_p=7.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+4y=7.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.
after.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}+4{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-4x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{-4x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{-4x})}^{′}+4(u{e}^{-4x}) & =7 \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-4x}-4u{e}^{-4x}+4u{e}^{-4x} & =7 \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-4x}-\cancel{4u{e}^{-4x}}+\cancel{4u{e}^{-4x}} & =7 \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-4x} & =7 \\ {u}^{′} & =7{e}^{4x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =7{e}^{4x} \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int 7{e}^{4x}\,\text{d}x \\ u & =\frac{7}{4}{e}^{4x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{-4x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{-4x} \\  & =\frac{7}{4}{e}^{4x}\cdot {e}^{-4x} \\  & =\frac{7}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the first-order linear ODE dydx+4y=7. We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form
u(x)e−4x
u(x)e−3x
u(x)e4x
u(x)e7x
u(x)e−7x
u(x)e−4x
.

Solving for u, we have u(x)=
74e4x
74e4x
73e3x
74e−4x
7e4x
14e4x
.

Therefore, the particular solution is yp(x)=
74
7e−4x
74
74e4x
14
−74
.
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution yc, we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by yc′+4yc=0.

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is yc=Ae−4x where A is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable yp, we set A=u(x) in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

yp(x)=u(x)e−4x

Intuitively, this form of yp tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find u, we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate u′:

(ue−4x)′+4(ue−4x)=7u′e−4x−4ue−4x+4ue−4x=7u′e−4x−4ue−4x+4ue−4x=7u′e−4x=7u′=7e4x

Integrating both sides with respect to x (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have u′=7e4x∫u′dx=∫7e4xdxu=74e4x.

Finally, since yp=u(x)e−4x, we have

yp=u(x)e−4x=74e4x⋅e−4x=74.

To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}+4{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-4x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{-4x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{-4x})}^{′}+4(u{e}^{-4x}) & =7 \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-4x}-4u{e}^{-4x}+4u{e}^{-4x} & =7 \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-4x}-\cancel{4u{e}^{-4x}}+\cancel{4u{e}^{-4x}} & =7 \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-4x} & =7 \\ {u}^{′} & =7{e}^{4x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =7{e}^{4x} \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int 7{e}^{4x}\,\text{d}x \\ u & =\frac{7}{4}{e}^{4x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{-4x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{-4x} \\  & =\frac{7}{4}{e}^{4x}\cdot {e}^{-4x} \\  & =\frac{7}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the first-order linear ODE dydx−y=2x−5. We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form
 
u(x)e5x
u(x)e−x
u(x)e−2x
u(x)e2x
u(x)ex
.

Solving for u, we have u(x)=
 
∫e−x(2x−5)dx
∫e−x(2x+5)dx
∫ex(2x−5)dx
∫e−x(5−2x)dx
.

Therefore, the particular solution is yp(x)=
 
e−x∫e−x(5−2x)dx
ex∫e−x(2x−5)dx
e−x∫ex(2x−5)dx
ex∫e−x(2x+5)dx
.
Submit

decision.explanation: The homogeneous equation y'-y=0 has solution Ce^x, so set y_p=u(x)e^x. Substitution gives u'e^x=2x-5, hence u'=e^{-x}(2x-5). Integrating yields the selected u and particular solution. Choosing the integration constant zero gives y_p=3-2x, whose derivative minus itself is 2x-5.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-y=2x-5.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.
after.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}-{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{x})}^{′}-(u{e}^{x}) & =2x-5 \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{x}+u{e}^{x}-u{e}^{x} & =2x-5 \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{x}+\cancel{u{e}^{x}}-\cancel{u{e}^{x}} & =2x-5 \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{x} & =2x-5 \\ {u}^{′} & ={e}^{-x}(2x-5)\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & ={e}^{-x}(2x-5) \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{-x}(2x-5)\,\text{d}x \\ u & =\int {e}^{-x}(2x-5)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{x} \\  & =\int {e}^{-x}(2x-5)\,\text{d}x\cdot {e}^{x} \\  & ={e}^{x}\int {e}^{-x}(2x-5)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the first-order linear ODE dydx−y=2x−5. We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form
u(x)e−2x
u(x)e5x
u(x)e−x
u(x)e−2x
u(x)e2x
u(x)ex
.

Solving for u, we have u(x)=
∫e−x(2x−5)dx
∫e−x(2x−5)dx
∫e−x(2x+5)dx
∫ex(2x−5)dx
∫e−x(5−2x)dx
.

Therefore, the particular solution is yp(x)=
ex∫e−x(2x−5)dx
e−x∫e−x(5−2x)dx
ex∫e−x(2x−5)dx
e−x∫ex(2x−5)dx
ex∫e−x(2x+5)dx
.
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution yc, we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by yc′−yc=0.

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is yc=Aex where A is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable yp, we set A=u(x) in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

yp(x)=u(x)ex

Intuitively, this form of yp tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find u, we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate u′:

(uex)′−(uex)=2x−5u′ex+uex−uex=2x−5u′ex+uex−uex=2x−5u′ex=2x−5u′=e−x(2x−5)

Integrating both sides with respect to x (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have u′=e−x(2x−5)∫u′dx=∫e−x(2x−5)dxu=∫e−x(2x−5)dx.

Finally, since yp=u(x)ex, we have

yp=u(x)ex=∫e−x(2x−5)dx⋅ex=ex∫e−x(2x−5)dx.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms y_p=u(x)e^x. Substitution gives u'e^x=2x-5, so u=∫e^{-x}(2x-5) dx and y_p=e^x∫e^{-x}(2x-5) dx. The deliberately incorrect submission used e^{-2x} in field-1; the earlier predicted answers remain correct.

content.knowledge_point: Solving First-Order Linear ODEs Using Variation of Parameters
content.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-y=2x-5.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.
content.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}-{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{x})}^{′}-(u{e}^{x}) & =2x-5 \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{x}+u{e}^{x}-u{e}^{x} & =2x-5 \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{x}+\cancel{u{e}^{x}}-\cancel{u{e}^{x}} & =2x-5 \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{x} & =2x-5 \\ {u}^{′} & ={e}^{-x}(2x-5)\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & ={e}^{-x}(2x-5) \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{-x}(2x-5)\,\text{d}x \\ u & =\int {e}^{-x}(2x-5)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{x} \\  & =\int {e}^{-x}(2x-5)\,\text{d}x\cdot {e}^{x} \\  & ={e}^{x}\int {e}^{-x}(2x-5)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-6y={e}^{6x}.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.
after.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}-6{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{6x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{6x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{6x})}^{′}-6(u{e}^{6x}) & ={e}^{6x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{6x}+6u{e}^{6x}-6u{e}^{6x} & ={e}^{6x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{6x}+\cancel{6u{e}^{6x}}-\cancel{6u{e}^{6x}} & ={e}^{6x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{6x} & ={e}^{6x} \\ {u}^{′} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =1 \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ u & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{6x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{6x} \\  & =x{e}^{6x}.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution yc, we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by yc′−6yc=0.

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is yc=Ae6x where A is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable yp, we set A=u(x) in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

yp(x)=u(x)e6x

Intuitively, this form of yp tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find u, we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate u′:

(ue6x)′−6(ue6x)=e6xu′e6x+6ue6x−6ue6x=e6xu′e6x+6ue6x−6ue6x=e6xu′e6x=e6xu′=1

Integrating both sides with respect to x (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have u′=1∫u′dx=∫dxu=x.

Finally, since yp=u(x)e6x, we have

yp=u(x)e6x=xe6x.

content.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-6y={e}^{6x}.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.
content.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}-6{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{6x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{6x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{6x})}^{′}-6(u{e}^{6x}) & ={e}^{6x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{6x}+6u{e}^{6x}-6u{e}^{6x} & ={e}^{6x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{6x}+\cancel{6u{e}^{6x}}-\cancel{6u{e}^{6x}} & ={e}^{6x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{6x} & ={e}^{6x} \\ {u}^{′} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =1 \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ u & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{6x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{6x} \\  & =x{e}^{6x}.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The homogeneous solution is Ce^{3x}, so set y_p=u(x)e^{3x}. Then u'=6e^{-3x}cosh(3x)=3(1+e^{-6x}). Integrating with constant zero gives u=3x-(1/2)e^{-6x}, hence y_p=3xe^{3x}-(1/2)e^{-3x}. This satisfies y_p'-3y_p=3e^{3x}+3e^{-3x}=6cosh(3x).

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3y=6\operatorname{cosh}⁡3x.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.
after.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}-3{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{3x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{3x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{3x})}^{′}-3(u{e}^{3x}) & =6\operatorname{cosh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{3x}+3u{e}^{3x}-3u{e}^{3x} & =6\operatorname{cosh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{3x}+\cancel{3u{e}^{3x}}-\cancel{3u{e}^{3x}} & =6\operatorname{cosh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{3x} & =6\operatorname{cosh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′} & =6{e}^{-3x}\operatorname{cosh}⁡3x\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\operatorname{cosh}⁡3x=\frac{{e}^{3x}+{e}^{-3x}}{2}
$$

our equation for $u$ becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =6{e}^{-3x}\operatorname{cosh}⁡3x \\  & =6{e}^{-3x}(\frac{{e}^{3x}+{e}^{-3x}}{2}) \\  & =3{e}^{-3x}({e}^{3x}+{e}^{-3x}) \\  & =3+3{e}^{-6x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =3+3{e}^{-6x} \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int 3+3{e}^{-6x}\,\text{d}x \\ u & =3x-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-6x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{3x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{3x} \\  & =3x{e}^{3x}-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-3x}.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution yc, we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by yc′−3yc=0.

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is yc=Ae3x where A is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable yp, we set A=u(x) in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

yp(x)=u(x)e3x

Intuitively, this form of yp tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find u, we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate u′:

(ue3x)′−3(ue3x)=6cosh⁡3xu′e3x+3ue3x−3ue3x=6cosh⁡3xu′e3x+3ue3x−3ue3x=6cosh⁡3xu′e3x=6cosh⁡3xu′=6e−3xcosh⁡3x

Using the fact that cosh⁡3x=e3x+e−3x2

our equation for u becomes

u′=6e−3xcosh⁡3x=6e−3x(e3x+e−3x2)=3e−3x(e3x+e−3x)=3+3e−6x.

Integrating both sides with respect to x (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have u′=3+3e−6x∫u′dx=∫3+3e−6xdxu=3x−12e−6x.

Finally, since yp=u(x)e3x, we have

yp=u(x)e3x=3xe3x−12e−3x.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms all three earlier answers. With y_p=u(x)e^{3x}, substitution gives u'=6e^{-3x}cosh(3x)=3+3e^{-6x}. Thus u=3x-(1/2)e^{-6x} and y_p=3xe^{3x}-(1/2)e^{-3x}. The deliberately incorrect submission changed only field-1 to the wrong exponential.

content.knowledge_point: Solving First-Order Linear ODEs Using VOP When the Forcing Term is Part of the Complementary Solution
content.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3y=6\operatorname{cosh}⁡3x.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.
content.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}-3{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{3x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{3x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{3x})}^{′}-3(u{e}^{3x}) & =6\operatorname{cosh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{3x}+3u{e}^{3x}-3u{e}^{3x} & =6\operatorname{cosh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{3x}+\cancel{3u{e}^{3x}}-\cancel{3u{e}^{3x}} & =6\operatorname{cosh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{3x} & =6\operatorname{cosh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′} & =6{e}^{-3x}\operatorname{cosh}⁡3x\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\operatorname{cosh}⁡3x=\frac{{e}^{3x}+{e}^{-3x}}{2}
$$

our equation for $u$ becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =6{e}^{-3x}\operatorname{cosh}⁡3x \\  & =6{e}^{-3x}(\frac{{e}^{3x}+{e}^{-3x}}{2}) \\  & =3{e}^{-3x}({e}^{3x}+{e}^{-3x}) \\  & =3+3{e}^{-6x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =3+3{e}^{-6x} \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int 3+3{e}^{-6x}\,\text{d}x \\ u & =3x-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-6x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{3x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{3x} \\  & =3x{e}^{3x}-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-3x}.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 5
?
Consider the first-order linear ODE dydx+5y=2e−x. We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form
 
u(x)e−5x
u(x)e−x
u(x)ex
u(x)e4x
u(x)e5x
.

Solving for u, we have u(x)=
 
12e4x
12e−4x
14e4x
2e4x
14e−6x
.

Therefore, the particular solution is yp(x)=
 
12e9x
2e−x
15e−5x
12e−x
14e−x
.
Submit

decision.explanation: The homogeneous solution is Ce^{-5x}, so set y_p=u(x)e^{-5x}. Substitution gives u'e^{-5x}=2e^{-x}, hence u'=2e^{4x} and u=(1/2)e^{4x}, omitting the integration constant. Thus y_p=(1/2)e^{-x}, which satisfies y_p'+5y_p=2e^{-x}.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+5y=2{e}^{-x}.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.

To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}+5{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-5x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{-5x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{-5x})}^{′}+5(u{e}^{-5x}) & =2{e}^{-x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-5x}-5u{e}^{-5x}+5u{e}^{-5x} & =2{e}^{-x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-5x}-\cancel{5u{e}^{-5x}}+\cancel{5u{e}^{-5x}} & =2{e}^{-x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-5x} & =2{e}^{-x} \\ {u}^{′} & =2{e}^{4x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =2{e}^{4x} \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int 2{e}^{4x}\,\text{d}x \\ u & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{4x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{-5x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{-5x} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{4x}\cdot {e}^{-5x} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution yc, we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by yc′+5yc=0.

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is yc=Ae−5x where A is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable yp, we set A=u(x) in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

yp(x)=u(x)e−5x

Intuitively, this form of yp tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find u, we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate u′:

(ue−5x)′+5(ue−5x)=2e−xu′e−5x−5ue−5x+5ue−5x=2e−xu′e−5x−5ue−5x+5ue−5x=2e−xu′e−5x=2e−xu′=2e4x

Integrating both sides with respect to x (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have u′=2e4x∫u′dx=∫2e4xdxu=12e4x.

Finally, since yp=u(x)e−5x, we have

yp=u(x)e−5x=12e4x⋅e−5x=12e−x.

content.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+5y=2{e}^{-x}.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.
content.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}+5{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-5x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{-5x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{-5x})}^{′}+5(u{e}^{-5x}) & =2{e}^{-x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-5x}-5u{e}^{-5x}+5u{e}^{-5x} & =2{e}^{-x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-5x}-\cancel{5u{e}^{-5x}}+\cancel{5u{e}^{-5x}} & =2{e}^{-x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-5x} & =2{e}^{-x} \\ {u}^{′} & =2{e}^{4x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =2{e}^{4x} \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int 2{e}^{4x}\,\text{d}x \\ u & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{4x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{-5x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{-5x} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{4x}\cdot {e}^{-5x} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-x}.\end{aligned}
$$
